title: Before the Key Turns: A Two-Person Fit Check for a Shared Car
subtitle: Daily Read — A quick, parked-car reset helps each driver check their own reach, belt, head restraint and mirrors before setting off.
imageAlt: Two partners sit in a parked car, one adjusting the driver’s seat while the other checks the mirror from the passenger side.
imageConcept: A candid, daylight scene of two partners of visibly different builds beside a parked shared car: one adjusts the driver’s seat and steering wheel while the other waits nearby with the owner’s manual in hand. The emphasis is on an ordinary, collaborative handoff, not a posed safety demonstration.
body: The car remembers one body at a time

A shared car can make the handoff feel automatic: one person gets out, the next gets in, and the trip continues. But a seat, steering wheel and set of mirrors arranged for one driver may not work for another. Differences in height, reach, mobility and preferred posture all matter; no single setup is the universal “correct” one. The useful habit is to treat each change of driver as a fresh fit check, done while the car is parked. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s driver-education materials frame vehicle fit as a set of adjustments—including pedal reach, head restraint and mirrors—to make before starting [1]. That turns the pause into more than a comfort tweak. It is a simple way to confirm that the person taking the wheel can reach the controls and see the road from their own position. If the car has memory settings, those can save time, but the driver still needs to check what the car has remembered.

Make the reset part of the handoff, not something to manage once the car is moving. Park securely, select the appropriate parking setting and let the incoming driver get settled before setting off. If the car is in a place where the driver cannot pause safely, wait until it is. The incoming driver can begin by sitting back in the seat and checking their view through the windshield and windows. Then adjust the seat and steering wheel so the controls are within comfortable reach and the road is clearly visible. NIOSH’s vehicle-fit checklist similarly includes a clear line of sight, access to the gas and brake pedals, and adjustments to the seat, belt and head restraint [2]. These are practical checks, not a test of whether someone is a “good” driver. The outgoing driver can help by leaving room and resisting the urge to make adjustments on the other person’s behalf. Each person should be able to judge their own view and reach.
Reach the controls, then settle the seat

With the car parked, check that you can operate the pedals without stretching or shifting forward in the seat. Confirm that you can move between the accelerator and brake with control. If reaching a pedal feels awkward, adjust the seat using the car’s controls, then test the reach again while stationary. Set the steering wheel as the owner’s manual directs, with the controls accessible and your view of the road and dashboard unobstructed. A different seat position may also change how the wheel feels in your hands, so revisit both rather than assuming one adjustment is enough. Make small changes, then pause and assess: Can you see clearly? Can you reach what you need without leaning? Does the position feel stable enough to operate the car? If the vehicle’s standard adjustments do not allow a safe, comfortable fit, do not try to solve it by improvising while driving. Check the manual for model-specific guidance; persistent fit problems or a need for adaptive equipment may call for help from a qualified driving specialist.
Check the belt and head restraint

Before moving, fasten the seat belt and check its path. The lap belt should fit snugly across the hips, and the shoulder belt should not be routed under the arm or behind the back [3]. Keep the belt flat, not twisted, and do not put the shoulder belt under an arm or behind the back. If it does not sit comfortably and correctly, check the vehicle manual for belt-height adjustment or other model-specific guidance. Then adjust the head restraint for the driver who is actually sitting there. Its position can change when the seat is moved, so a setting left by the previous driver is not a reliable check. NIOSH includes both the belt and head restraint in its vehicle-fit checklist [2]. That checklist was prepared for older workers, but the adjustments it identifies are relevant here as practical items to verify—not a reason to assume anything about a driver’s ability based on age. The owner’s manual remains the place to confirm how a particular restraint is meant to be adjusted.
Set the mirrors from your own seat

Mirrors are part of the incoming driver’s setup, not a shared setting to leave untouched. Sit in the position you plan to drive in, then adjust the rearview and side mirrors so they give you a useful view from that seat. If you change the seat after setting the mirrors, check them again. AAA’s Via article describes setting mirrors from the driver’s position and notes that correctly adjusted mirrors still cannot eliminate every blind spot [3]. So a good mirror view is not a promise that everything beside or behind the car is visible. Before moving off, make sure you understand the car’s sightlines; when driving, use the appropriate direct side check as well as the mirrors before changing lanes or moving into a space. A mirror set for the last driver may leave the next person with a different view, even if the glass itself has not moved much. Taking a moment to reset it is more useful than trying to adapt to somebody else’s angles.
Let presets save time, not replace judgment

A memory preset can be a convenient first move, especially when two people trade the same car often. But it is a stored position, not a confirmation that the driver is ready to go. The seat may have been moved manually since the preset was saved; the steering wheel or mirrors may not be included in that setting; and the driver’s needs can change from one trip to the next. The practical takeaway is modest: use the preset if it helps, then check the fit yourself.
Make the handoff part of the trip

For the next shared-car trip, try a repeatable two-minute sequence while parked: the incoming driver adjusts the seat and steering wheel, checks pedal reach and visibility, fastens and checks the belt, adjusts the head restraint, and sets the mirrors. The outgoing driver can ask, “Anything you want me to leave in a different position next time?” rather than deciding what the other person needs. If you share the driving regularly, agree on a simple convention: leave the car safely parked, avoid changing another person’s setup without asking, and give the next driver time to reset. A preset can be a useful starting point; the person driving has the final check. At the end of the next handoff, make one small note together: which adjustment is easy to forget, and where the manual explains it? Keep the answer somewhere practical, such as a shared phone note. The aim is not a perfect ritual or a score for either driver. It is a clear, low-pressure pause that puts the next person’s reach and view first.
